title: Easing: why animations look robotic
creator: Unnamed (promo for the Ugoki motion course)
one_liner: Nothing real moves at constant speed: ease out entrances, ease in exits, spring the interface, nothing linear.
why_it_matters: Every text pop, rep counter, zoom and pan in your reels is an animation, and the default in most tools (and in our own ffmpeg builds) is linear, which reads as cheap. Three rules and a four-line prompt make every motion feel hand-placed, whether you keyframe in Edits/CapCut or ask Claude to build it.

big_idea.statement: Animations look robotic because they move at constant speed; give every movement a curve that matches what it's doing.
support: In the real world nothing starts or stops instantly, so linear motion looks fake.
Things arriving should arrive fast and brake slowly (ease out).
Things leaving should start slowly and then get away (ease in).
Interface elements should spring: overshoot slightly, then settle.
Saying these exact words to Claude upgrades any AI-built motion.

chapters.title: The problem is speed
chapters.summary: The video opens with a question about a pain point, 'Does your animation look robotic?', over a side-by-side of a ROBOT slider and a PRO slider. The diagnosis: the problem is its speed. Nothing in the real world moves at a constant speed, but a linear animation does. A dotted trail behind the moving object makes this visible: every step is the same distance apart, so it starts all at once and stops all at once.

blocks.text: Nothing in the real world moves at a constant speed.

right.title: PRO (eased)
items: Dots bunch up where it slows

blocks.text: To spot linear motion in your own edit, scrub frame by frame: if the object moves the same distance every frame, it's linear.

chapters.title: Three rules for three kinds of motion
chapters.summary: Each kind of motion gets its own curve. Everything that comes in should ease out: it arrives fast, then brakes for a long time, as if set down by a steady hand. Everything that leaves gets the opposite, ease in: it starts slowly, then gets away. And for the interface (buttons, cards, pop-ups, labels) use a spring: it overshoots its target just a little, then settles back.

blocks.title: Match the curve to the job

items.label: Entrances → ease out

items.label: Interface → spring
items.text: Overshoots a little, then settles back.

blocks.text: Gym reel: the '75 KG' label eases out as it lands, the rep counter springs (slight overshoot) on each rep, and the old text eases in as it leaves. Gaming: the kill-feed style text springs; the scoreboard slides in with ease out.

chapters.title: The four-line prompt
chapters.summary: The reusable part is a prompt shown on screen. The narrator says to tell Claude in exactly these words, and your animation jumps to a whole new level. It's four short lines that cover entrances, exits, interface elements and a ban on linear motion. It works the same for HyperFrames, Remotion, CSS or any tool where an AI writes the motion.

blocks.text: Tell Claude in exactly these words, and your animation jumps to a whole new level.

blocks.title: Asking an AI for a rep counter
blocks.before: Make a counter that goes from 0 to 75 kg and a label that slides in.
blocks.after: Make a counter that goes from 0 to 75 kg and a label that slides in. Entrances: ease out. Exits: ease in. Interface: spring, slight overshoot. Nothing linear.
blocks.why: Without the four lines, most tools default to linear or a generic ease. With them, the label lands, the counter settles and nothing moves like a robot.

chapters.title: How the video teaches it
chapters.summary: The video is faceless and all motion graphics. The hook pairs the pain question with visual proof: ROBOT vs PRO sliders side by side. Position-versus-time graphs with dotted trails turn an abstract idea into something you can see. Captions appear one word at a time in white bold sans, with the key word in a red highlight box ('speed.', 'out.', 'brakes'). The palette is near-black with a red glow and red as the only accent. A new caption word lands every 0.3–0.5 s while the graph animates continuously with no cuts. It ends on a locked card for the Ugoki course and 'DM me UGOKI' typed into a DM box.

chapters.title: Fixing our own edits
chapters.summary: Our own Khandala reel breaks the rule: the photo pans and push-ins in the ffmpeg build move at constant speed. The fix is to ease every pan and zoom: ease out on moves that arrive, ease in on exits. In Edits, CapCut or VN, keyframes have ease curves; in ffmpeg, replace the plain t/d progress with an eased expression. The rep-counter pop in the incline reel was already close to a spring (fast in, settle), so that stays.

blocks.title: An ffmpeg push-in
blocks.before: zoom = 1 + 0.1 × (t/d)  (linear: same zoom step every frame)
blocks.after: zoom = 1 + 0.1 × (1 − (1 − t/d)³)  (cubic ease out: fast start, long gentle stop)
blocks.why: Same start and end zoom; only the speed curve changes, and the move now 'lands'.

blocks.title: Easing audit for every reel
items: Each pan and push-in: eased, not linear?
Counters, labels, cards: spring with slight overshoot?
Any element moving at constant speed? Fix it.

blocks.text: In Edits/CapCut: add two keyframes, tap the curve between them and pick an ease-out preset for anything arriving. For your gym clips, a slow eased push-in on the final rep sells the effort.

takeaways.text: Entrances ease out, exits ease in.
UI and text pops spring with a slight overshoot.
Paste the four-line easing prompt whenever an AI builds motion.
Our Khandala pans and push-ins were linear: ease them.
Make motion visible with a dotted trail or graph.
Word-by-word captions with the key word highlighted.
Hook with a pain question plus side-by-side visual proof.

glossary.def: Changing an animation's speed over time instead of moving at constant speed.
Constant speed from start to finish; looks robotic.
Fast at the start, slowing to a gentle stop. For things arriving.
Slow at the start, speeding up. For things leaving.
Motion that overshoots its target slightly, then settles back. For interface elements.
Going a little past the end position before settling.
A point in time where you set a value (position, scale); the editor animates between keyframes.
Dots showing where an object was on each frame; even spacing means linear motion.

quiz.q: Why do linear animations look robotic?
quiz.a: Nothing real moves at constant speed; linear motion starts and stops all at once.

quiz.q: Which curve for something entering the frame?
quiz.a: Ease out: arrives fast, brakes for a long time.
Ease in: starts slowly, then gets away.
Spring: overshoot slightly, then settle back.

quiz.q: What does an evenly spaced dotted trail tell you?

quiz.a: Entrances: ease out. Exits: ease in. Interface: spring, slight overshoot. Nothing linear.

try_it.title: Ease a gym reel
steps: Open your last gym edit in Edits or CapCut.
Find every keyframed move (zoom, pan, text slide).
Set arrivals to ease out and exits to ease in.
Make the weight label spring in with a slight overshoot.
Compare old vs new side by side.

try_it.title: Robot vs pro hook for a tech reel
steps: Animate the same spec card twice: once linear, once with the four-line prompt.
Place them side by side, labelled ROBOT and PRO.
Open the reel on that comparison and ask 'Does your edit look robotic?'

try_it.title: Spring your gaming overlays
steps: Make a kill-count or rank label overlay.
Ask Claude (or keyframe) with the four-line prompt.
Add a pop SFX on the overshoot frame.
Check it frame by frame: no constant-speed moves.
